einzeiler: Exploring the origins of the First Amendment and the evolution of the free press in…
kurzfassung: This episode examines the history of the First Amendment, focusing on the freedom of the press and its vital role in holding power accountable. Co-hosts Greg Jackson and Lindsay Cormack trace this constitutional right from colonial publisher John Peter Zenger's landmark trial through the ratification of the Bill of Rights. The discussion also features guest expert Mitchell Kramer exploring Benjamin Franklin's views on truth, media partisanship, and historical parallels to modern debates over fake news.
stichpunkte: John Peter Zenger's 1735 trial established an early precedent for a free press when a jury acquitted him of seditious libel for criticizing New York's governor.
The First Amendment was not part of the original Constitution but was added as part of the Bill of Rights pushed by James Madison.
Initial interpretations of the First Amendment viewed it strictly as a limitation on the federal government, not state governments.
Historical media in America has predominantly been partisan rather than purely objective, dating back to the colonial era.
Scholars and founders recognized that a government strong enough to enforce media objectivity would also be strong enough to suppress legitimate criticism.
Benjamin Franklin and other founders separated the pursuit of scientific truth from the entertaining and politically motivated nature of colonial newspapers.
Despite periods of heavy-handed legislation like the Sedition Act of 1798 and intense partisan attacks, the American press has continuously served as an external check on government power.

clips.hook: True or not, to criticize the government in print is itself a crime.
clips.text: Under colonial legal standards, publishing factual criticisms about government corruption was treated as a punishable offense regardless of its accuracy.

clips.hook: Massachusetts was using tax dollars to fund churches all the way into the 1830s.
clips.text: State governments maintained official religious establishments long after the federal Constitution was ratified, as the Bill of Rights initially applied only to Congress.
Congressional district sizes have expanded dramatically over time from early proposals of smaller representation ratios.

clips.hook: Do you love truth for truth's sake?
clips.text: Colonial-era scientific societies opened their meetings with an explicit pledge to impartially pursue and communicate objective truth.

clips.hook: 1876 could arguably be one of the worst years in American history.
clips.text: The nation faced a convergence of severe crises during its centennial celebration, yet ultimately persevered through those turbulent times.

beschreibung:
In 1735, a colonial printer named John Peter Zenger spent nine months in jail for printing someone else's criticism of a corrupt governor, and his trial helped plant the seeds of a free press in America decades before the First Amendment existed. This episode, we trace the origins of press freedom, why "fake news" is a much older problem than you'd think, and why the Constitution protects the printer, not the truth — plus a conversation with historian Mitchell Kramer on what Benjamin Franklin really thought about truth and partisanship in the press.
